title: the Rudram
hook: after all the bowing, the Rudram's companion turns around and asks, line after line, and to me

segments.voice: Yesterday the Rudram went outdoors: green-haired trees, rain and drought, the foam at the edge of the water. What overlooked thing did you look at twice? Day one thousand one hundred fifty-one.
screen: `THE FOAM IS HOLY.` · `TODAY: THE OTHER HALF.`

segments.voice: Rice. Barley. Beans. Sesame. Wheat. Lentils. It sounds like a grocery list taped to a fridge. It's a Vedic hymn. When the Rudram is chanted in full, tradition pairs the bowing half, the Namakam, with a companion, the Chamakam. And the Chamakam does something the Namakam never did. It asks. Line after line, ending again and again with two small words: cha me. And to me. Today, the half of the hymn that holds out its hands.
screen: `RICE, BARLEY, BEANS, SESAME.` → `A GROCERY LIST?` → `CHA ME — AND TO ME.`

segments.voice: The Namakam is built on namah, a bow. The Chamakam is built on cha me, and to me. It's a long list of requests, each one tagged with those two words. And what it asks for is startling in how ordinary it is. Strength, and to me. Ease and comfort, and to me. What is dear, and to me. Then food. Milk and the sap of plants. Ghee and honey. Rice and barley, beans and sesame, wheat and lentils. Plowing, and rain. And two worth stopping on: eating together, and drinking together. The hymn asks for company at the table. There's something honest about that. After bowing to Rudra in every corner of the world, the chanter doesn't pretend to need nothing. They name what a body and a household actually need. Grain in the pot. Rain on the field. People to share it with. One way to hear the two halves is as a pair, like breathing. The Namakam breathes out: everything belongs to Rudra, and I bow. The Chamakam breathes in: and from all that, may this come to me. Neither half is complete without the other. A life of only bowing could float away from the kitchen. A life of only asking would forget whom it's asking. And notice the tone of the asking. There's no shame in it. The chanter has bowed to Rudra in the drought and the lightning. Now, in the companion verses, they ask plainly for lentils. In this pairing, the hymn that bows to the storm sits right beside the one that asks for dinner, and for someone to eat it with.
screen: `CHA ME — AND TO ME.` · `GRAIN, RAIN, GHEE AND HONEY.` · `EATING TOGETHER, DRINKING TOGETHER.` · `BOWING OUT, ASKING IN.` · then, large: `ASKING FOR LENTILS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name what you need. Sit, and let the breath settle. Without judging the list, let a few plain needs come up. Not big wishes. Ordinary things. Sleep. A good meal. Someone to eat it with. Rain, if your garden is dry. Name each one quietly, and let it rest there, held out, the way the Chamakam holds it out. Then, on the out-breath, let the list go. If you pray, you can offer these needs to Shiva, in your own words. The bell holds the time.
The Rudram. Today, its companion, the Chamakam: cha me, and to me, asking plainly for grain, rain, and company at the table.
Your line: the Rudram. Today, share one meal or one drink with someone on purpose, even a coffee, and let it be the thing the hymn asked for. Day one thousand one hundred fifty-one.

howItsDone: When the Shri Rudram is chanted in full, tradition pairs the Namakam with the Chamakam, and both are recited in Vedic Sanskrit, at home, in temples and during abhishekam.
